- "CSR — what is sent and what never leaves" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Certificate Signing Request. Applicant generates the key pair FIRST, then sends a CSR containing the PUBLIC key plus subject/organisation details, self-signed with the matching private key to prove possession. The PRIVATE KEY NEVER LEAVES THE APPLICANT — never in the CSR, never to the CA, never in the issued certificate. CA validates (DNS record, verification email, web-file placement, or organisation documents), then signs the certificate with the CA's private key; the applicant installs the returned cert on the server. Two flagged traps: (1) "the applicant sends the private key in the CSR" — wrong, and it is the classic distractor; (2) "the certificate contains the private key" — wrong, an X.509 cert carries the public key. Related but distinct: a PFX/P12 bundle DOES contain the private key, which is why it is password-protected — that is a storage format, not the CSR or the certificate.
- "SAN vs Wildcard certificates" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Two different ways to cover more than one name, routinely confused. SAN (Subject Alternative Name) = an X.509 EXTENSION listing additional specific identities — DNS names, IP addresses, email addresses — and can span entirely different domains (www.example.com + mail.example.net). Wildcard = a single asterisk label, *.example.com, covering many subdomains. Wildcard limits the exam tests: (1) ONE label level only — *.example.com matches mail.example.com but NOT server.mail.example.com; (2) it does not automatically cover the bare root domain example.com, which must be listed separately as a SAN. Security tradeoff worth knowing: one wildcard private key deployed across many servers means a single compromise exposes every service using it, so separate certificates buy isolation at the cost of management overhead. Hostname matching is what browsers actually check — the visited name must match the Subject or one of the SAN entries.
- "Revocation: CRL vs OCSP vs OCSP Stapling" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Three answers to "is this certificate still trusted?", distinguished by WHO does the work. CRL = client DOWNLOADS a CA-published list of revoked serial numbers; simple and offline-checkable, but the file grows large and the data is only as fresh as the last publication. OCSP = client ASKS an OCSP responder about ONE certificate and gets good / revoked / unknown; current, but adds a network round trip, loads the CA, fails awkwardly when the responder is down, and leaks the client's browsing to the responder. OCSP STAPLING = the SERVER periodically fetches a CA-SIGNED status response and attaches ("staples") it to the TLS handshake; removes the client-to-CA request entirely, so it is faster, scales better and restores client privacy. Flagged trap: stapling does NOT mean the server vouches for itself — the stapled response carries the CA's digital signature, which the client verifies. Second trap: expiration is not revocation. A certificate inside its validity window can still be revoked (key compromise, mis-issuance, ownership change), which is exactly why revocation checking exists.
- "Public vs Private CA + chain of trust" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Public/third-party CA = its root certificate already ships in browser and OS trust stores, so external users trust the certificate with no action; used for public HTTPS, e-commerce, public APIs. Private/internal CA (AD Certificate Services, enterprise PKI, cloud private CA) = the organisation issues its own certificates for internal sites, domain controllers, VPN and Wi-Fi authentication, device and user certs, code signing. Flagged trap: a private CA is NOT automatically trusted — the organisation must DISTRIBUTE its root certificate to every device's trust store, or users get certificate warnings. Validation path: end-entity certificate signed by an Intermediate CA, intermediate signed by the Root CA, root already present in the trust store. Intermediates exist so the root can stay offline; a root compromise invalidates every certificate beneath it. Flagged trap: the root does NOT sign end-entity certificates directly in normal enterprise or public PKI. Remember the CA operation is SIGNING, not encrypting — it provides authentication, integrity and trust, not confidentiality of the site's traffic.
- "The six threat actors and their one-word tells" (Threat Actors & Motivations / obj 2.1) — SY0-701 2.1 names exactly six actors, and each has one clue that resolves most scenario questions on its own. NATION-STATE = GOVERNMENT (espionage, critical infrastructure, cyberwarfare; very high resources; long dwell; the archetype behind APT campaigns). UNSKILLED ATTACKER = TOOLS AND TUTORIALS (formerly "script kiddie"; runs other people's exploits without understanding them; low resources; motivations run to curiosity, recognition, chaos). HACKTIVIST = BELIEFS (political, social or ideological cause; wants publicity; defacement, DDoS, doxing and leaks; variable resources). INSIDER THREAT = TRUSTED ACCESS (employee, contractor, administrator or partner; motivations include revenge, money, espionage). ORGANIZED CRIME = MONEY (ransomware, fraud, extortion, credential and identity theft; run as a business with developers, launderers and even victim support desks; high resources). SHADOW IT = UNAPPROVED TECH (staff adopting tools IT has not sanctioned, usually for convenience rather than malice). Memorise the order as N-U-H-I-O-S. Two attributes to carry alongside: INTERNAL origin covers insider threat and Shadow IT only — the other four are characteristically external; and the rough resource ordering runs nation-state, then organized crime, then hacktivist, then unskilled, which is a tendency and not a rule. Two traps the exam leans on: a sophisticated TOOL does not make a sophisticated ATTACKER, and an insider need be neither malicious nor an employee — negligence counts, and so do contractors and trusted partners.
- "Threat actor vs motivation vs vector — three separate answers" (Threat Actors & Motivations / obj 2.1) — Security+ deliberately blurs three distinct questions, and a scenario often supplies all three at once. THREAT ACTOR answers WHO is behind it — the person, group or entity. MOTIVATION answers WHY — the objective they are pursuing. THREAT VECTOR answers HOW THEY GOT IN — the route into the environment. The attack or malware deployed afterwards is a fourth thing again, and is none of the three. Worked example: a criminal gang phishes employees, steals credentials, deploys ransomware and demands two million pounds. Actor = organized crime. Motivation = financial gain, with blackmail. Vector = email (the phishing message). Attack = ransomware. The motivations named in the objective are data exfiltration (stealing information), espionage (covert intelligence gathering), service disruption (taking systems offline), blackmail (pay or we release), financial gain (making money), philosophical or political beliefs (supporting a cause), ethical (security research and responsible disclosure), revenge (retaliation), disruption or chaos (damage for its own sake), and war (attacking another state's capabilities). Read the question wording carefully: "which threat actor", "what motivated", and "how did the attacker gain access" are three different questions with three different answers from the same scenario, and the wrong options are usually the right answers to the other two.
- "The phishing family: P-S-W-S-V-B, then WHO vs STORY" (Social Engineering / obj 2.2) — Six variants, each resolved by one tell. PHISHING = PUBLIC: a mass blast priced on volume — "Dear customer", thousands of recipients, the sender does not care that most have no such account. SPEAR PHISHING = SPECIFIC: the message knows something about you (your name, your team, your supplier), because reconnaissance came first. WHALING = WEALTHY target: spear phishing whose recipient is an executive or other high-value target — the C-suite is the whale. SMISHING = SMS. VISHING = VOICE. BEC = BUSINESS MONEY: a trusted business identity (an executive, or a genuinely compromised supplier mailbox) borrowed to push a fraudulent transaction through the person who can approve it. Memorise the order as P-S-W-S-V-B. Then the two component techniques that appear INSIDE the variants: IMPERSONATION answers WHO the attacker claims to be ("I am David from IT"); PRETEXTING is the STORY that makes the request feel routine ("we are migrating MFA this afternoon"). One attack stacks several — a single call can be vishing + impersonation + pretexting at once. Two reading rules for the exam: (1) the delivery channel picks the variant name — the same lure is phishing by email, smishing by SMS, vishing by phone; (2) when several answers are technically present, pick the MOST SPECIFIC — the ladder runs phishing, then spear phishing, then whaling or BEC, and the question "who is the victim, whose name is borrowed?" separates those last two: executive as TARGET = whaling, executive as MASK = BEC.
- "The emotional levers and the out-of-band check" (Social Engineering / obj 2.2) — Phishing works by making the target react emotionally instead of checking carefully. The levers: URGENCY ("within 15 minutes"), FEAR — the classical principle name is INTIMIDATION ("your account is compromised", "to avoid prosecution"), GREED ("you have received a refund"), AUTHORITY ("the CEO needs this now"), TRUST/FAMILIARITY (a borrowed brand or colleague identity), CURIOSITY ("confidential salary list"), SYMPATHY ("please donate"), plus two more from CompTIA's classical persuasion list: SOCIAL PROOF/CONSENSUS ("everyone else on the team has already confirmed") and SCARCITY ("only three licence renewals left"). Spotting the lever is often faster than spotting the forgery — any message engineered to make you act before you think deserves a second look regardless of how clean it appears. The defence that defeats the whole family: OUT-OF-BAND VERIFICATION — confirm the request over a DIFFERENT channel the attacker does not control, using contact details you ALREADY HOLD, never ones supplied in the message ("call the CEO back on the number on file", not the number in the email signature). It matters most where technical checks legitimately pass: in the supplier invoice-swap BEC, the mail leaves the supplier's real mailbox, SPF and DKIM succeed, the invoice is genuine and only the account number changed — a standing rule that every change to payment details is verified out-of-band against contact details already on file — with dual approval of payment changes as its natural companion — is the class of control that dependably still works. Related mechanical tells worth pairing with the levers: lookalike domains (typosquatting — paypa1 with a digit 1), pixel-perfect copied login pages (brand impersonation), a Reply-to that differs from the sender domain, and a post-theft redirect to the real site so the victim blames a typo and never reports.
- "Vector vs surface, and the four buckets" (Attack Vectors & Surfaces / obj 2.2) — Four questions untangle most scenario stems. WHO attacked = threat actor. WHY = motivation. HOW did they reach you = threat vector. WHERE COULD they have = attack surface. The house picture holds the last two apart: every door, window, garage and chimney together is the attack surface; the one unlocked window the burglar actually used is the threat vector. Shrinking the surface (closing ports, removing services, decommissioning old systems) narrows the attacker's options without eliminating the routes that remain open. Then group the SY0-701 vector list into four recallable buckets. DELIVERY — something is sent or carried to you: messages (email, SMS, instant messaging), images (SVG carrying script), files (macro documents, archives, executables), voice calls, removable devices. TECHNOLOGY — a weakness waits to be found: vulnerable software (client-based = installed on the endpoint; agentless = reached through a browser, so the flaw lives centrally), unsupported systems past vendor end of life, unsecure networks (wireless, wired, Bluetooth — the wall jack counts), open service ports, default credentials. TRUST — something already trusted is turned: supply chain through MSPs, vendors and suppliers, and the watering-hole site your team already visits. HUMAN — the social-engineering family, held in the Social Engineering retention entries. One scenario often crosses buckets: a phishing email carrying a macro spreadsheet is DELIVERY twice over — message-based vector, file-based payload container.
- "Vector recognition tells + the two traps" (Attack Vectors & Surfaces / obj 2.2) — The exam names the vector through one operational detail — learn the tells as reflexes. USB found in the car park = removable device. admin/admin still working = default credentials. Vendor stopped patching = unsupported system (remediation is architectural: replace, isolate, compensate — no download is coming). Unneeded RDP or SSH reachable from the internet = open service port growing the attack surface. Script inside an SVG executing on view = image-based. Teams, Slack or SMS delivery = message-based, exactly like email. Live Ethernet jack in a public room = unsecure wired (the fix that names itself: 802.1X port-based network access control). Nearby attacker and a weak pairing protocol = unsecure Bluetooth. Many unrelated victims sharing one service provider = supply chain through the MSP, because one provider compromise inherits the admin access every customer already granted. Then the two traps. TRAP ONE: an open port is exposure, not a vulnerability — 443 open on a web server is the machine doing its job; risk concentrates in ports nobody needs and in vulnerable or misconfigured services behind open ones. TRAP TWO: vulnerable is not unsupported — vulnerable software has a patch available but unapplied (an operations failure, fixed by updating), while an unsupported system has no patch coming from the vendor (an architecture problem, fixed by upgrading or isolating). The remediation path is what the exam is really asking for.
- "The attack chain: OSINT learns, impersonation pretends, pretexting explains, spoofing falsifies, phishing delivers" (Social Engineering / obj 2.2) — Five roles the exam keeps separate, easiest read as a chain. OSINT LEARNS — public-source homework (LinkedIn, company site, press releases, WHOIS, breach dumps) that makes the later contact believable. IMPERSONATION PRETENDS — the WHO: claiming to be the CEO, IT, a vendor. PRETEXTING EXPLAINS — the STORY: the invented reason to act ("I am overseas and cannot call"). SPOOFING FALSIFIES — the technical identity: a forged From header, a faked caller ID, a spoofed sending domain (distinct from typosquatting, which REGISTERS a similar-looking domain rather than falsifying an existing one). PHISHING DELIVERS — the fraudulent message that carries it all to the victim (email = phishing, SMS = smishing, voice = vishing). One incident routinely contains several: a spoofed CEO email (spoofing) impersonating the CEO (impersonation) with a confidential-acquisition story (pretexting) built from LinkedIn research (OSINT) asking for a wire transfer (a likely BEC). Two rules the exam rewards: deepfakes (AI-cloned voice or video) raise the CREDIBILITY of impersonation but never change the defence; and the defence is out-of-band verification — confirm the request through a separate channel and a contact detail you already hold, because replying "are you really the CEO?" on the same channel still talks to the attacker.
- "OSINT: passive vs active, and intent-neutral" (Audits & Assessments / obj 5.5) — OSINT is intelligence from publicly accessible sources, and it is overwhelmingly PASSIVE reconnaissance: reading LinkedIn, WHOIS and DNS records, news, job postings and public records touches nothing the target owns. ACTIVE reconnaissance interacts with the target's own systems — a port scan, service enumeration, probing a web app — and that is the line a port scan crosses. Passive = looking from outside; active = knocking on the doors to see which open. Two exam points beyond the split. First, OSINT is intent-neutral and lawful: the technique is defined by the source type, not the actor, so a threat-intelligence team searching paste sites for leaked credentials and brand-abuse profiles is doing exactly the same OSINT an attacker does, for the opposite reason — same information, different intent. Second, the danger is AGGREGATION: one LinkedIn profile, one Instagram post, one job advert each look harmless, but combined they yield people + technologies + timing + relationships, and a job posting that lists the security stack (Entra ID, Sentinel, CrowdStrike, a named firewall) hands an attacker the environment for free. Public does not mean harmless.

EXEMPLAR 2:
Question: A vulnerability scan reports a critical, remotely exploitable flaw on a file server. A manager concludes the server has been compromised. Is that right?
A) Yes, because a critical finding means an attacker has already exploited it
B) Yes, because scanners only report flaws that they have actively exploited
C) No, because a critical finding is always a false positive until it is patched

B) The IDS log
C) The DNS log
D) The DHCP log
Answer: D

HONEYFILE = a single FAKE FILE in a real production share (named to attract attackers; fires alert on access). HONEYTOKEN = the UMBRELLA term for any seeded fake data unit (fake DB records, fake API keys, fake credentials, fake email addresses, watermarked docs) — honeyfile is a subset. Scope ladder: honeypot (system) → honeynet (network of systems) → honeyfile (one file) → honeytoken (any data unit, broadest).
- "DNS Sinkhole" (Security Controls / obj 1.2) — Recursive DNS resolver is configured with a list of known-bad domains (C2, phishing, malware-distribution). When a client queries one, the resolver returns a controlled response — typically a null IP, dedicated sinkhole VLAN address, or security-team-controlled honeypot — instead of the real DNS answer. Two simultaneous wins: (1) PREVENTS the infected client from reaching real C2 infrastructure, (2) DETECTS infected hosts via the resolver query logs. Limitation: hard-coded IPs (no DNS lookup) bypass it; still need firewall + IDS for those.
- "Deception vs Disruption" (Security Controls / obj 1.2) — DECEPTION = lure and observe (defender creates fake assets/data and waits for attackers to engage — honeypot, honeynet, honeyfile, honeytoken, fake telemetry). DISRUPTION = active interference with attacker operations (DNS sinkhole redirecting C2, RPZ poisoning, beacon jamming, exfiltration-path latency injection). Many controls bridge both — e.g., DNS sinkhole that redirects to a honeypot is BOTH disruption (real C2 fails) AND deception (attacker now talks to your decoy). Both are DEFENSIVE — active offensive counter-hacking is legally murky and not in SY0-701 Domain 1.2.
- "Change Management Workflow" (Change Management / obj 1.3) — RFC submission → impact analysis + risk assessment → CAB review/approval → sandbox/staging testing → scheduled maintenance window with backout plan READY → implementation → post-implementation review (PIR). Skipping any step degrades change management to "paperwork over cowboy ops." The PIR is the learning loop — without it, the org stops getting better at change.
- "Ownership vs Stakeholders vs CAB" (Change Management / obj 1.3) — RACI-driven distinction. OWNER = single accountable person driving the change to completion (one per change, no co-owners — accountability cannot be diffused). STAKEHOLDERS = the broader set informed/consulted (affected user groups, dependent service owners, security/compliance, support teams). CAB (Change Advisory Board / Change Control Board) = the cross-functional review body that approves/rejects/defers — composition should span security, operations, business owners, technical leads, and (when relevant) compliance/legal. CAB is NOT a technical-only body.
- "Backout Plan as Approval Gate" (Change Management / obj 1.3) — Every production change requires a documented, tested BACKOUT (ROLLBACK) plan — regardless of how thorough the testing was. Testing reduces failure probability but cannot eliminate prod surprises (real data shapes, concurrent load, third-party behavior, network conditions). The backout plan is the answer to "when something goes wrong, how do we restore service?" — includes pre-change backup, scripted rollback procedure, decision time-budget, verification steps. "We tested thoroughly" is not a substitute. Also distinguish from MAINTENANCE WINDOW (the WHEN of implementation, not the recovery procedure) and from SOPs (repeatable routine procedures, not one-off change rollbacks).
- "Allow List vs Deny List" (Technical Change Management / obj 1.3) — Application-control models, and BOTH are change-management concerns. ALLOW LIST = DEFAULT-DENY: nothing runs unless explicitly approved (by file hash, digital signature, publisher, or path). Blocks unknown/novel malware by definition. Cost: high admin overhead — a legitimate update changes the hash/version, so the allow-list policy must be updated AS PART OF the change or the app silently fails to launch. DENY LIST = DEFAULT-ALLOW: everything runs unless it matches a known-bad indicator (classic signature AV). Easier to operate, less restrictive, but structurally cannot block a threat it has never seen. Exam trap: "deny listing is stronger" is FALSE — allow listing is the more restrictive/secure model.
- "Approved Scope & Restricted Activities" (Technical Change Management / obj 1.3) — Approval is SPECIFIC, never a general licence to modify. An approved change names the systems in scope, the actions authorized, the personnel, and the time limits — everything else is a RESTRICTED ACTIVITY. Approval to upgrade the PRIMARY firewall does NOT authorize upgrading the secondary, deleting stale rules, replacing hardware, or touching routing. When implementation reveals unforeseen work (e.g. the app upgrade also needs a driver upgrade), the correct move is SCOPE EXPANSION THROUGH APPROVAL: pause, document the new requirement, notify the change owner, obtain expanded authorization, or invoke the backout plan. Fixing it unilaterally "because it was necessary" is uncontrolled scope creep — it bypasses the impact analysis the CAB actually performed and can invalidate the backout plan. Exam trap: "approval means permission to fix anything I discover."
- "Downtime, Restarts & Availability Techniques" (Technical Change Management / obj 1.3) — Downtime primarily attacks AVAILABILITY (CIA). PLANNED downtime must be scheduled, communicated (start, duration, systems, impact, contact), minimized, and monitored. AVOIDING downtime uses redundancy: failover, ROLLING UPGRADE, blue-green deployment, HA maintenance — drain traffic off node A, upgrade + validate it, shift traffic to it, then upgrade node B. The un-upgraded node doubles as the rollback path. SERVICE RESTART / APPLICATION RESTART are their own named technical implication: many services read config only at START-UP, so a saved config file is NOT live until restart (or an explicit reload signal) — and the restart itself drops sessions, so it must be a planned, communicated, validated step in the procedure. Automation (scripts, IaC, templates) reduces human error and increases repeatability, but a faulty automated change propagates errors fast, so automation must itself be tested and approved.
- "Dependencies, Order & Legacy Applications" (Technical Change Management / obj 1.3) — DEPENDENCY = something another system requires to function (web app -> database; service -> DNS; auth -> identity provider; managed firewall -> compatible management platform). ORDER MATTERS, and the rule is: derive the supported sequence from the VENDOR COMPATIBILITY MATRIX. The common case is MANAGER-FIRST — the management platform must support the version running on the managed device, so upgrading the device code first can strand it behind an incompatible manager, costing you management, monitoring, and the ability to roll back through normal tooling. Always keep out-of-band access (console/serial) as a safety net. HIDDEN (undocumented) dependencies are the dangerous ones: restarting a certificate server breaks device ENROLLMENT (issuance needs the CA online), and breaks VPN / 802.1X only where REVOCATION CHECKING (OCSP responder or CRL distribution point, usually co-hosted on the CA) becomes unreachable and relying parties hard-fail — 802.1X itself terminates at RADIUS/NPS. Dependency maps + current architecture diagrams are the countermeasure. LEGACY APPLICATION = old, often unsupported/unpatchable, but frequently BUSINESS-CRITICAL — "legacy" does NOT mean "useless". Routine estate-wide changes (TLS hardening, OS patch, password policy) can silently break them, so flag them in impact analysis. Interim posture: COMPENSATING CONTROLS — segmentation, strict firewall rules, application allow listing, restricted admin access, enhanced monitoring, limited internet exposure, more frequent backups — while replacement is planned.
- "Documentation, Version Control & Validation" (Technical Change Management / obj 1.3) — A change is complete when the RECORDED state matches the ACTUAL state, not when the installer exits 0. Exam trap: "a successful installation means a successful change" is FALSE — you must VALIDATE the intended result, that security controls / logging / monitoring still function, that users can reach the service, and that no side effects hit dependent systems. Then update DOCUMENTATION as part of the change (never "next quarter"): network + data-flow diagrams, asset inventory, firewall rule and IP/DNS records, procedures, policies, system baselines, dependency maps, recovery instructions. Stale docs degrade incident response, troubleshooting, audit, DR, and — compounding — the impact analysis of every FUTURE change. VERSION CONTROL on configs/scripts/IaC gives change history, author + timestamp accountability, version diffing, approval/review workflow before merge, and restoration of an earlier known-good revision (a component of the backout plan). It does NOT make a change secure, and it does NOT remove the need for a maintenance window.
- "PICERL Incident Response Order" (Incident Response / obj 4.8) — Preparation -> Identification -> Containment -> Eradication -> Recovery -> Lessons Learned. Memorize as P-I-C-E-R-L. Order is exam-tested in drag-and-drop PBQs. Preparation FIRST (cannot respond well without prep). Containment BEFORE eradication (stop spread, then remove threat). Lessons Learned LAST (drives improvement, often skipped which leaves orgs vulnerable to repeat incidents).
- "RTO vs RPO vs MTTR vs MTBF" (Risk Management / obj 5.2) — BC/DR vs reliability metric distinction. RTO = max acceptable downtime (target). RPO = max acceptable data loss (target). MTTR = mean time to repair (measured statistic). MTBF = mean time between failures (measured statistic). RTO/RPO are TARGETS the org sets. MTTR/MTBF are MEASURED statistics about hardware. Confusing these four is a classic exam trap.
- "DMARC + DKIM + SPF email-trio" (Email & Web Security / obj 4.5) — Domain anti-spoofing trio. SPF (Sender Policy Framework) = which servers are authorized to SEND from this domain (IP-based, TXT record). DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) = cryptographic SIGNATURE on the message body (verifies integrity). DMARC = POLICY on what to do when SPF/DKIM fail alignment (none / quarantine / reject) + reporting. Together they detect + act on domain spoofing in inbound email.
- "Tactical vs Operational vs Strategic Threat Intel" (Attack Vectors & Surfaces / obj 2.2) — Three threat intelligence tiers, distinguished by consumer + content. Tactical = TTPs and IOCs (analyst consumers - hashes, IPs, signatures). Operational = campaign context and adversary tooling (responder consumers - kill chains, TTPs in context). Strategic = business risk and adversary motivation (executive consumers - geopolitical risk, sector trends). VoC S12 surprise - ExamTopics flagged this as confusable.
- "Certificate Format Families" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Cert file format distinctions. PEM = base64 ASCII (.pem/.crt) - human-readable, most common. DER = binary (.der/.cer) - compact, common on Windows. PFX/P12 (PKCS#12) = public + private key + chain in ONE password-protected file (.pfx/.p12) - for importing into Windows/macOS keychains. P7B (PKCS#7) = chain ONLY, no private key (.p7b). Exam tests choosing the right format for the use case.
- "AAA Framework" (Identity & Access Management / obj 4.6) — Three-pillar identity framework. Authentication = WHO you are (verify identity via password, MFA, biometrics, cert). Authorization = WHAT you can do (permissions, RBAC/ABAC/MAC/DAC decision). Accounting = WHAT you did (audit log, session tracking). Often implemented as RADIUS / TACACS+ services. Exam stems mix these - identify which pillar is being tested.
- "Risk Math: ALE = SLE × ARO" (Risk Management / obj 5.2) — Fundamental quantitative-risk formula. SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) = $ cost of one loss event. ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) = how many times per year. ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy) = SLE × ARO = expected yearly $ loss. Drives risk-treatment cost-benefit: spending more than ALE on mitigation per year is net-negative. Also Exposure Factor (EF) = % of asset value lost per event; SLE = Asset Value × EF.
- "OWASP Top 3 Web App Risks" (Application Vulnerabilities / obj 2.3) — OWASP Top 10 current top 3: 1. Broken Access Control (auth checks missing/bypassable). 2. Cryptographic Failures (weak/missing encryption, exposed sensitive data). 3. Injection (SQLi, LDAP, OS-command injection - tainted input executed as code). Each maps to distinct mitigations: access control = central authorization, principle of least privilege; crypto failures = TLS + at-rest encryption + key management; injection = parameterized queries + input validation + output encoding.
- "Blockchain & Open Public Ledger" (Cryptography Fundamentals / obj 1.4) — Two 1.4 bullets, tested at recognition level. Blockchain = distributed ledger where each block carries the PREVIOUS block's hash, so altering an accepted record changes its digest, breaks every later link, and is rejected by consensus. Property delivered = INTEGRITY (plus non-repudiation via per-transaction digital signatures, and availability via replication across nodes). Property NOT delivered = CONFIDENTIALITY — an open public ledger is readable by all participants, addresses are pseudonymous not anonymous, so sensitive data belongs off-chain with only a hash on-chain. Two flagged traps: (1) "immutable" means tamper-EVIDENT, not physically unalterable; (2) integrity of the record ≠ truth of the claim — a signed false entry is preserved perfectly ("garbage in, immutable garbage out"). Not cryptocurrency-specific: supply chain, identity, audit and ownership records are the exam's usual framing.
- "CSR — what is sent and what never leaves" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Certificate Signing Request. Applicant generates the key pair FIRST, then sends a CSR containing the PUBLIC key plus subject/organisation details, self-signed with the matching private key to prove possession. The PRIVATE KEY NEVER LEAVES THE APPLICANT — never in the CSR, never to the CA, never in the issued certificate. CA validates (DNS record, verification email, web-file placement, or organisation documents), then signs the certificate with the CA's private key; the applicant installs the returned cert on the server. Two flagged traps: (1) "the applicant sends the private key in the CSR" — wrong, and it is the classic distractor; (2) "the certificate contains the private key" — wrong, an X.509 cert carries the public key. Related but distinct: a PFX/P12 bundle DOES contain the private key, which is why it is password-protected — that is a storage format, not the CSR or the certificate.
- "SAN vs Wildcard certificates" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Two different ways to cover more than one name, routinely confused. SAN (Subject Alternative Name) = an X.509 EXTENSION listing additional specific identities — DNS names, IP addresses, email addresses — and can span entirely different domains (www.example.com + mail.example.net). Wildcard = a single asterisk label, *.example.com, covering many subdomains. Wildcard limits the exam tests: (1) ONE label level only — *.example.com matches mail.example.com but NOT server.mail.example.com; (2) it does not automatically cover the bare root domain example.com, which must be listed separately as a SAN. Security tradeoff worth knowing: one wildcard private key deployed across many servers means a single compromise exposes every service using it, so separate certificates buy isolation at the cost of management overhead. Hostname matching is what browsers actually check — the visited name must match the Subject or one of the SAN entries.
- "Revocation: CRL vs OCSP vs OCSP Stapling" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Three answers to "is this certificate still trusted?", distinguished by WHO does the work. CRL = client DOWNLOADS a CA-published list of revoked serial numbers; simple and offline-checkable, but the file grows large and the data is only as fresh as the last publication. OCSP = client ASKS an OCSP responder about ONE certificate and gets good / revoked / unknown; current, but adds a network round trip, loads the CA, fails awkwardly when the responder is down, and leaks the client's browsing to the responder. OCSP STAPLING = the SERVER periodically fetches a CA-SIGNED status response and attaches ("staples") it to the TLS handshake; removes the client-to-CA request entirely, so it is faster, scales better and restores client privacy. Flagged trap: stapling does NOT mean the server vouches for itself — the stapled response carries the CA's digital signature, which the client verifies. Second trap: expiration is not revocation. A certificate inside its validity window can still be revoked (key compromise, mis-issuance, ownership change), which is exactly why revocation checking exists.
- "Public vs Private CA + chain of trust" (PKI & Certificate Management / obj 1.4) — Public/third-party CA = its root certificate already ships in browser and OS trust stores, so external users trust the certificate with no action; used for public HTTPS, e-commerce, public APIs. Private/internal CA (AD Certificate Services, enterprise PKI, cloud private CA) = the organisation issues its own certificates for internal sites, domain controllers, VPN and Wi-Fi authentication, device and user certs, code signing. Flagged trap: a private CA is NOT automatically trusted — the organisation must DISTRIBUTE its root certificate to every device's trust store, or users get certificate warnings. Validation path: end-entity certificate signed by an Intermediate CA, intermediate signed by the Root CA, root already present in the trust store. Intermediates exist so the root can stay offline; a root compromise invalidates every certificate beneath it. Flagged trap: the root does NOT sign end-entity certificates directly in normal enterprise or public PKI. Remember the CA operation is SIGNING, not encrypting — it provides authentication, integrity and trust, not confidentiality of the site's traffic.
- "The six threat actors and their one-word tells" (Threat Actors & Motivations / obj 2.1) — SY0-701 2.1 names exactly six actors, and each has one clue that resolves most scenario questions on its own. NATION-STATE = GOVERNMENT (espionage, critical infrastructure, cyberwarfare; very high resources; long dwell; the archetype behind APT campaigns). UNSKILLED ATTACKER = TOOLS AND TUTORIALS (formerly "script kiddie"; runs other people's exploits without understanding them; low resources; motivations run to curiosity, recognition, chaos). HACKTIVIST = BELIEFS (political, social or ideological cause; wants publicity; defacement, DDoS, doxing and leaks; variable resources). INSIDER THREAT = TRUSTED ACCESS (employee, contractor, administrator or partner; motivations include revenge, money, espionage). ORGANIZED CRIME = MONEY (ransomware, fraud, extortion, credential and identity theft; run as a business with developers, launderers and even victim support desks; high resources). SHADOW IT = UNAPPROVED TECH (staff adopting tools IT has not sanctioned, usually for convenience rather than malice). Memorise the order as N-U-H-I-O-S. Two attributes to carry alongside: INTERNAL origin covers insider threat and Shadow IT only — the other four are characteristically external; and the rough resource ordering runs nation-state, then organized crime, then hacktivist, then unskilled, which is a tendency and not a rule. Two traps the exam leans on: a sophisticated TOOL does not make a sophisticated ATTACKER, and an insider need be neither malicious nor an employee — negligence counts, and so do contractors and trusted partners.
- "Threat actor vs motivation vs vector — three separate answers" (Threat Actors & Motivations / obj 2.1) — Security+ deliberately blurs three distinct questions, and a scenario often supplies all three at once. THREAT ACTOR answers WHO is behind it — the person, group or entity. MOTIVATION answers WHY — the objective they are pursuing. THREAT VECTOR answers HOW THEY GOT IN — the route into the environment. The attack or malware deployed afterwards is a fourth thing again, and is none of the three. Worked example: a criminal gang phishes employees, steals credentials, deploys ransomware and demands two million pounds. Actor = organized crime. Motivation = financial gain, with blackmail. Vector = email (the phishing message). Attack = ransomware. The motivations named in the objective are data exfiltration (stealing information), espionage (covert intelligence gathering), service disruption (taking systems offline), blackmail (pay or we release), financial gain (making money), philosophical or political beliefs (supporting a cause), ethical (security research and responsible disclosure), revenge (retaliation), disruption or chaos (damage for its own sake), and war (attacking another state's capabilities). Read the question wording carefully: "which threat actor", "what motivated", and "how did the attacker gain access" are three different questions with three different answers from the same scenario, and the wrong options are usually the right answers to the other two.
- "The phishing family: P-S-W-S-V-B, then WHO vs STORY" (Social Engineering / obj 2.2) — Six variants, each resolved by one tell. PHISHING = PUBLIC: a mass blast priced on volume — "Dear customer", thousands of recipients, the sender does not care that most have no such account. SPEAR PHISHING = SPECIFIC: the message knows something about you (your name, your team, your supplier), because reconnaissance came first. WHALING = WEALTHY target: spear phishing whose recipient is an executive or other high-value target — the C-suite is the whale. SMISHING = SMS. VISHING = VOICE. BEC = BUSINESS MONEY: a trusted business identity (an executive, or a genuinely compromised supplier mailbox) borrowed to push a fraudulent transaction through the person who can approve it. Memorise the order as P-S-W-S-V-B. Then the two component techniques that appear INSIDE the variants: IMPERSONATION answers WHO the attacker claims to be ("I am David from IT"); PRETEXTING is the STORY that makes the request feel routine ("we are migrating MFA this afternoon"). One attack stacks several — a single call can be vishing + impersonation + pretexting at once. Two reading rules for the exam: (1) the delivery channel picks the variant name — the same lure is phishing by email, smishing by SMS, vishing by phone; (2) when several answers are technically present, pick the MOST SPECIFIC — the ladder runs phishing, then spear phishing, then whaling or BEC, and the question "who is the victim, whose name is borrowed?" separates those last two: executive as TARGET = whaling, executive as MASK = BEC.
- "The emotional levers and the out-of-band check" (Social Engineering / obj 2.2) — Phishing works by making the target react emotionally instead of checking carefully. The levers: URGENCY ("within 15 minutes"), FEAR — the classical principle name is INTIMIDATION ("your account is compromised", "to avoid prosecution"), GREED ("you have received a refund"), AUTHORITY ("the CEO needs this now"), TRUST/FAMILIARITY (a borrowed brand or colleague identity), CURIOSITY ("confidential salary list"), SYMPATHY ("please donate"), plus two more from CompTIA's classical persuasion list: SOCIAL PROOF/CONSENSUS ("everyone else on the team has already confirmed") and SCARCITY ("only three licence renewals left"). Spotting the lever is often faster than spotting the forgery — any message engineered to make you act before you think deserves a second look regardless of how clean it appears. The defence that defeats the whole family: OUT-OF-BAND VERIFICATION — confirm the request over a DIFFERENT channel the attacker does not control, using contact details you ALREADY HOLD, never ones supplied in the message ("call the CEO back on the number on file", not the number in the email signature). It matters most where technical checks legitimately pass: in the supplier invoice-swap BEC, the mail leaves the supplier's real mailbox, SPF and DKIM succeed, the invoice is genuine and only the account number changed — a standing rule that every change to payment details is verified out-of-band against contact details already on file — with dual approval of payment changes as its natural companion — is the class of control that dependably still works. Related mechanical tells worth pairing with the levers: lookalike domains (typosquatting — paypa1 with a digit 1), pixel-perfect copied login pages (brand impersonation), a Reply-to that differs from the sender domain, and a post-theft redirect to the real site so the victim blames a typo and never reports.
- "Vector vs surface, and the four buckets" (Attack Vectors & Surfaces / obj 2.2) — Four questions untangle most scenario stems. WHO attacked = threat actor. WHY = motivation. HOW did they reach you = threat vector. WHERE COULD they have = attack surface. The house picture holds the last two apart: every door, window, garage and chimney together is the attack surface; the one unlocked window the burglar actually used is the threat vector. Shrinking the surface (closing ports, removing services, decommissioning old systems) narrows the attacker's options without eliminating the routes that remain open. Then group the SY0-701 vector list into four recallable buckets. DELIVERY — something is sent or carried to you: messages (email, SMS, instant messaging), images (SVG carrying script), files (macro documents, archives, executables), voice calls, removable devices. TECHNOLOGY — a weakness waits to be found: vulnerable software (client-based = installed on the endpoint; agentless = reached through a browser, so the flaw lives centrally), unsupported systems past vendor end of life, unsecure networks (wireless, wired, Bluetooth — the wall jack counts), open service ports, default credentials. TRUST — something already trusted is turned: supply chain through MSPs, vendors and suppliers, and the watering-hole site your team already visits. HUMAN — the social-engineering family, held in the Social Engineering retention entries. One scenario often crosses buckets: a phishing email carrying a macro spreadsheet is DELIVERY twice over — message-based vector, file-based payload container.
- "Vector recognition tells + the two traps" (Attack Vectors & Surfaces / obj 2.2) — The exam names the vector through one operational detail — learn the tells as reflexes. USB found in the car park = removable device. admin/admin still working = default credentials. Vendor stopped patching = unsupported system (remediation is architectural: replace, isolate, compensate — no download is coming). Unneeded RDP or SSH reachable from the internet = open service port growing the attack surface. Script inside an SVG executing on view = image-based. Teams, Slack or SMS delivery = message-based, exactly like email. Live Ethernet jack in a public room = unsecure wired (the fix that names itself: 802.1X port-based network access control). Nearby attacker and a weak pairing protocol = unsecure Bluetooth. Many unrelated victims sharing one service provider = supply chain through the MSP, because one provider compromise inherits the admin access every customer already granted. Then the two traps. TRAP ONE: an open port is exposure, not a vulnerability — 443 open on a web server is the machine doing its job; risk concentrates in ports nobody needs and in vulnerable or misconfigured services behind open ones. TRAP TWO: vulnerable is not unsupported — vulnerable software has a patch available but unapplied (an operations failure, fixed by updating), while an unsupported system has no patch coming from the vendor (an architecture problem, fixed by upgrading or isolating). The remediation path is what the exam is really asking for.
- "The attack chain: OSINT learns, impersonation pretends, pretexting explains, spoofing falsifies, phishing delivers" (Social Engineering / obj 2.2) — Five roles the exam keeps separate, easiest read as a chain. OSINT LEARNS — public-source homework (LinkedIn, company site, press releases, WHOIS, breach dumps) that makes the later contact believable. IMPERSONATION PRETENDS — the WHO: claiming to be the CEO, IT, a vendor. PRETEXTING EXPLAINS — the STORY: the invented reason to act ("I am overseas and cannot call"). SPOOFING FALSIFIES — the technical identity: a forged From header, a faked caller ID, a spoofed sending domain (distinct from typosquatting, which REGISTERS a similar-looking domain rather than falsifying an existing one). PHISHING DELIVERS — the fraudulent message that carries it all to the victim (email = phishing, SMS = smishing, voice = vishing). One incident routinely contains several: a spoofed CEO email (spoofing) impersonating the CEO (impersonation) with a confidential-acquisition story (pretexting) built from LinkedIn research (OSINT) asking for a wire transfer (a likely BEC). Two rules the exam rewards: deepfakes (AI-cloned voice or video) raise the CREDIBILITY of impersonation but never change the defence; and the defence is out-of-band verification — confirm the request through a separate channel and a contact detail you already hold, because replying "are you really the CEO?" on the same channel still talks to the attacker.
- "OSINT: passive vs active, and intent-neutral" (Audits & Assessments / obj 5.5) — OSINT is intelligence from publicly accessible sources, and it is overwhelmingly PASSIVE reconnaissance: reading LinkedIn, WHOIS and DNS records, news, job postings and public records touches nothing the target owns. ACTIVE reconnaissance interacts with the target's own systems — a port scan, service enumeration, probing a web app — and that is the line a port scan crosses. Passive = looking from outside; active = knocking on the doors to see which open. Two exam points beyond the split. First, OSINT is intent-neutral and lawful: the technique is defined by the source type, not the actor, so a threat-intelligence team searching paste sites for leaked credentials and brand-abuse profiles is doing exactly the same OSINT an attacker does, for the opposite reason — same information, different intent. Second, the danger is AGGREGATION: one LinkedIn profile, one Instagram post, one job advert each look harmless, but combined they yield people + technologies + timing + relationships, and a job posting that lists the security stack (Entra ID, Sentinel, CrowdStrike, a named firewall) hands an attacker the environment for free. Public does not mean harmless.

CRITICAL — MULTI-SELECT QUALITY CRITERIA (CompTIA exam style):
- BOTH (or all 3) correct answers must be CORE, well-known facts about the topic — at similar levels of prominence/familiarity. Do NOT make one correct answer obvious and the other obscure or edge-case. Difficulty in multi-select comes from BREADTH (knowing multiple facts apply), NOT from one being a buried trivia point.
- DISTRACTORS must be FACTUALLY WRONG about the topic. They should describe things that are categorically false, NOT things that are "less correct" or are correct facts about an adjacent/related topic. The user must be able to rule them out with actual knowledge — not by elimination.
- AVOID the trap of "1 obvious correct + 1 obscure correct + 2 plausible-sounding adjacent-topic distractors" — that produces partial-credit scoring and frustration without testing real understanding.
- The EXPLANATION must enumerate, separately and concretely:
  • WHY each correct answer is correct (1-2 sentences each)
  • WHY each distractor is wrong — naming a specific factual error, not just "less applicable" or "not the best fit"
- Multi-select stems should ask about what IS true / IS valid / DOES apply — not about ranking, fit, or "best."
- Every correct answer must apply to the stem AS WRITTEN — never one that needs a scenario the stem doesn't mention (e.g. a BEC-only control as a correct answer to a generic "phishing" stem). If you want to test it, put the scenario in the stem.
- NEVER create a question where MORE options are factually correct than the stem asks for. Example: 6to4, Teredo, AND NAT64 are ALL valid IPv6 transition methods — a "Which TWO" stem forces the student to guess which 2 of 3 correct answers the grader prefers, which is NOT how CompTIA writes exams. If a topic has N valid answers, either ask for all N or reframe the stem to narrow which subset is being tested (e.g., "Which TWO are tunneling methods?" excludes NAT64 since it's translation, not tunneling).
- SELF-TEST before finalizing: for each correct answer, ask "could a student who studied this topic for 2 weeks identify this as correct?" If the answer is no for ANY correct option, the question fails the balance test. Replace the obscure correct answer with a more recognizable one.
- CONCRETE EXAMPLES of good vs bad multi-select:
  BAD: "Which TWO describe OSPF?" → A) Uses Dijkstra's algorithm (obvious) B) Uses area 0 as backbone (obscure detail) — student gets A easily, guesses on B.
  GOOD: "Which TWO are link-state routing protocols?" → A) OSPF B) IS-IS — both are CORE facts at the same prominence level. A student who studied routing protocols knows both.
  BAD: "Which TWO are used for network monitoring?" → A) SNMP (obvious) B) NetFlow (less obvious) C) Syslog (also valid!) — 3 correct answers crammed into "pick 2."
  GOOD: "Which TWO protocols use UDP port 161 or 162?" → A) SNMP GET B) SNMP TRAP — narrow, factual, both equally knowable.

CRITICAL — SELF-VERIFICATION PROTOCOL (you MUST follow these steps for EVERY question):
Step 1: Write the question and all options.
Step 2: INDEPENDENTLY determine which option is factually correct by reasoning through the technical concept. Do NOT just pick a letter — think through WHY.
Step 3: Set the "answer" field to the letter of the option you verified in Step 2.
Step 4: Write the explanation referencing that SAME letter and option text.
Step 5: CROSS-CHECK: Re-read the option text at your chosen answer letter. Does it match what your explanation says? If not, fix the answer field.
Step 6: PREMISE-ANSWER CONSISTENCY CHECK: Re-read the question stem. Does the correct answer CONTRADICT any fact explicitly stated in the stem? If the stem says "both devices are on VLAN 30", the answer CANNOT be "they are on different VLANs." If you find a contradiction, rewrite the question or change the answer so the stem and answer are logically consistent.

MANDATORY RULES:
- The "answer" field must ALWAYS match the letter whose option text is factually correct
- The "explanation" must explicitly reference why the correct option is right and why at least one wrong option is wrong
- If you notice ANY mismatch between answer letter, option text, and explanation — fix it before outputting
- Never output a question where the explanation and the answer field disagree

CONCEPTUAL COHERENCE RULES (v4.57.0 — enforce rigorously):
- Do NOT conflate deprecated classful addressing (Class A/B/C) with modern TCP/IP or CIDR/subnet principles. Classful addressing was obsoleted by CIDR in 1993 (RFC 1519). If you reference classful terminology, it must be explicitly about legacy concepts or historical context — never framed as a "fundamental TCP/IP principle."
- Do NOT conflate distinct concepts under one label. If the stem asks about "a TCP/IP principle," the answer must be about the TCP/IP protocol stack (layers, encapsulation, ports, the four-layer model), not about IP address classes. If the stem asks about "an OSI Layer 3 function," the answer must actually be a Layer 3 function, not a Layer 2 one.
- MATCH THE ABSTRACTION LEVEL: If the stem asks for a "principle," "fundamental concept," or "root cause," the answer must be at that level of abstraction — NOT a specific configuration step or tool. ("Default gateway not configured" is a configuration detail, not a principle.) If the stem asks for a specific fix or symptom, don't give an abstract principle.
- NO UNSTATED SCENARIOS: A correct answer must be correct for the stem AS WRITTEN. If an option is only right under a specific scenario or attack variant the stem never mentions (e.g. stem asks about "phishing" but the answer is "out-of-band verification of payment changes", which only fits business email compromise / invoice fraud), either name that scenario in the stem or don't use the option as a correct answer. The student must never have to invent context to reach the key.
- STEM MUST MATCH WHAT THE QUESTION ACTUALLY TESTS: If the stem says "which protocol operates at Layer 3?", the question must test Layer 3 protocol knowledge — not addressing theory, not encapsulation. Read your own stem and make sure the answer directly addresses what you asked.

DISTRACTOR QUALITY RULES:
- At least TWO of the three wrong options must be plausible-enough to tempt a student who only partially knows the material. If 3 of 4 options are obviously wrong (e.g. completely unrelated or factually nonsensical), the question becomes a giveaway that doesn't test real knowledge.
- Distractors should represent common misconceptions, adjacent concepts, or nearly-right answers — not random unrelated facts.

STEM MUST BE AN ACTUAL QUESTION (v4.57.2):
- The "question" field MUST contain a real interrogative, not pure declarative setup. Either end with "?" OR use explicit question words: "which", "what", "why", "how", "when", "where", or CompTIA-style imperatives: "Select the...", "Identify the...", "Choose the...", "Arrange these in order", "Place each device in the correct...", "Match each protocol with...", "Given the scenario, which...".
- ❌ WRONG: "A system administrator is deploying a remote access VPN solution that requires users to authenticate and access corporate resources through a web browser without installing additional VPN client software." (This is pure setup. No question is asked. The learner has no cue what to pick.)
- ✅ RIGHT: "A system administrator is deploying a remote access VPN that must work from any browser without installing client software. **Which VPN type best fits this requirement?**"
- If you want to include setup context, put it in the OPTIONAL "scenario" field — but the "question" field itself MUST still pose a direct question. Scenario + question is additive; scenario is never a substitute for the question.
